sections.h2: Where is Marion, Iowa, and how did it start?
sections.html:
Marion is a city in Linn County that sits right beside Cedar Rapids and belongs to the Cedar Rapids metropolitan area. It was incorporated in 1837 and takes its name from Francis Marion, a Revolutionary War figure.

The site was chosen in 1839 as the first county seat of the newly organized Linn County. That role ended after a 1919 vote moved the seat to Cedar Rapids, 9,960 to 4,823. Marion kept its own identity anyway, and the older streets near the Granger House Museum (a restored 1840s Victorian home with an 1879 carriage house) still show how early the town was laid out.

The town sits at about 840 feet of elevation, and the ZIP code is 52302. A seller here is usually dealing with a mix of older uptown houses and the newer subdivisions that came with fast growth.

Marion grew from 26,294 residents in 2000 to 41,535 in 2020, a gain of about 58 percent, and the Census Bureau estimates 42,732 as of July 1, 2025. That makes it one of the faster-growing cities in the state.

A 77.4 percent owner-occupancy rate means most Marion houses are lived in by their owners. Rentals are a smaller slice, but they are regulated closely, as the rental section below explains.

Three public districts reach into the city: the Marion Independent School District, the Linn-Mar Community School District and the Cedar Rapids Community School District. Marion Independent covers the south and east sides, while Linn-Mar covers the north, west and far east sides and runs Linn-Mar High School.

Private options include St. Joseph School, which was founded in 1947 and serves preschool through eighth grade, and Grace Baptist School for kindergarten through twelfth grade. If you are selling, find out which district a house falls in before you describe it to a buyer. Two houses a few blocks apart can sit in different districts, and families often ask first.

sections.h2: What do the roads and transit mean for a Marion house?
sections.html:
U.S. Route 151 and Iowa Highway 13 both run north and south through Marion, and Seventh Avenue is the main arterial toward Cedar Rapids. Cedar Rapids Transit Bus Route 20 serves the city, and a small public airport sits on the east edge of the city limits south of U.S. 151.

Because Marion is next door to Cedar Rapids, a house here can be a short drive from jobs on either side of the line. A house near Seventh Avenue or the highway corridors is easy to reach, and some buyers will weigh road noise against that.

  • U.S. 151 and Iowa 13 for north and south trips
  • Seventh Avenue for the run toward Cedar Rapids
  • Route 20 for bus riders
  • Local airport on the east side, south of U.S. 151

sections.h2: What is the weather like in Marion, and what does it do to a house?
sections.html:
Marion has cold winters and hot summers: the average January high is about 30 degrees and the average July high is about 85.5 degrees. Annual precipitation averages 38.75 inches, and snowfall averages 34.3 inches. Records run from 110 degrees in July to minus 33 in January.

Those swings are hard on roofs, gutters, furnaces and basements. A buyer's inspector will look at attic ventilation, ice damage at the eaves and any sign of water in the lower level. The county has also been through the June 2008 Cedar River flooding and the August 2020 derecho, so many buyers ask about past storm repairs and whether claims were paid.

If you own a house with deferred roof or basement work, a cash sale as-is lets you skip the repair bids and the back and forth over inspection credits.

sections.h2: What are Marion's rental housing rules?
sections.html:
Marion requires owners to register rental units and hold a landlord license, and every rental dwelling is subject to inspection roughly every two years. The city counts a unit as a rental even when family or friends live there without paying rent.

The rules matter to a seller for two reasons. A landlord selling a tenant-occupied house may need to tell the city the unit is no longer theirs, and a buyer who plans to rent it will have to register it. The city charges fees for licenses, inspections, missed inspections and confirmed complaints, and the amounts are not published on the page we reviewed. Marion Rental Housing can be reached at 319-200-1299.

  • Register a new rental, or tell the city you no longer have one
  • Complete the online landlord license renewal before a license is issued
  • Expect an inspection about every two years, plus extra visits after complaints
  • Single-family houses, rooming houses and group residences are all covered

Iowa law pushes cities of this size in the same direction. Under Iowa Code 364.17, a city that adopts a rental program must include regular rental inspections, may charge reasonable fees, and can add a late penalty and interest to unpaid fees. Unpaid amounts can turn into a lien on the property after notice.

sections.h2: What do Marion's museums and events say about the neighborhoods?
sections.html:
Marion's older core is built around its historic sites. Besides the Granger House, the Marion Heritage Center occupies a former Methodist church building and holds a 1939 fresco mural titled Communication by Mail.

Annual events draw visitors and keep uptown busy: the Swamp Fox Festival and Parade honors Francis Marion, the Marion Arts Festival is a one-day event with about 50 artists, and the Uptown Marion Market runs with produce, baked goods and live entertainment. The Marion Economic Development Corporation, a public-private partnership, has worked on business growth since 1984.

For a seller, age matters. A house near the historic uptown core and a house in a subdivision built during the recent growth years are different products, and a cash offer will weigh the age of the roof, furnace and wiring in either one.

sections.h2: How are Linn County property taxes billed for a Marion house?
sections.html:
Linn County bills property tax in two halves, due September 1 and March 1, and a half becomes delinquent on October 1 or April 1. Mailed payments need the stub and a postmark by September 30 or March 31 to avoid a late fee.

The Linn County Treasurer is at 935 Second Street SW in Cedar Rapids, and payments can be made online at Iowataxandtags.org, by mail, in person, by phone at 319-892-5500, or in the drop box outside the Public Service Center. Iowa Code 445.37 sets the delinquency dates and moves them to the second business day of the month when the day before falls on a weekend.

At closing, the title company normally works out which share of the current installment belongs to you and which to the buyer. Ask for the paid receipts so you know nothing is left behind.

sections.h2: What does Iowa require when a Marion house is sold?
sections.html:
The deed is recorded with the county recorder, and a declaration of value must be signed by at least one buyer or seller at that time. Iowa also charges real estate transfer tax of 80 cents for each $500 of value above the first $500, under Iowa Code 428A.1.

As an illustration only, the owner-occupied median value of $241,700 works out like this: $241,700 minus $500 is $241,200, divided by $500 is 482.4, rounded up to 483, times $0.80 gives $386.40. Your own number depends on the price actually paid, and the tax is due when the deed is presented for recording.

  • Signed deed
  • Declaration of value
  • Transfer tax at recording
  • Payoff letters for any mortgage or lien
  • Tax proration between buyer and seller

sections.h2: How does a cash sale of a Marion house work?
sections.html:
A cash sale means a buyer pays without a mortgage, so there is no lender appraisal or loan underwriting to wait for. You ask for an offer, we look at the house and the title, you decide, and closing is scheduled with a title company on a date that suits you.

That can matter in Marion if the house needs work, has a tenant with a lease, or came to you through an estate. It also suits owners who want to avoid showings and open houses. A cash buyer will look at the repairs a house needs and reflect them in the offer, so compare any offer with what you would net from a listing after repairs, commissions and time on the market.

We make no promise about price before we see the property, and you can say no.

faqs.q: Do I need to register my Marion rental before I sell it?
faqs.a: Marion requires registration and a landlord license for rentals, and you should tell the city when you no longer own the unit. The buyer will need to register if they plan to rent it. Call Marion Rental Housing at 319-200-1299 to confirm what applies to your address.

faqs.q: When are Linn County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Linn County property taxes are due September 1 and March 1. They become delinquent on October 1 and April 1, and a mailed payment needs a postmark by September 30 or March 31.

faqs.q: What is the Iowa transfer tax on a house sale?
faqs.a: It is 80 cents for each $500 of value above the first $500, under Iowa Code 428A.1. The county recorder collects it when the deed is presented, and a declaration of value is filed at the same time.

faqs.q: Which school district is my Marion house in?
faqs.a: It depends on the street. Marion Independent covers the south and east sides, Linn-Mar covers the north, west and far east sides, and parts of the city fall in the Cedar Rapids district. Check the address with the district before you tell buyers.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Marion house that needs major repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. Cash buyers purchase houses as-is, so roof, foundation, water damage and outdated systems do not have to be fixed first. The offer reflects the condition, and you decide whether to accept it.

faqs.q: Why did Marion stop being the county seat?
faqs.a: Voters moved the Linn County seat to Cedar Rapids in a 1919 election, 9,960 to 4,823. Marion had been the first county seat after the site was chosen in 1839.
